# Veilfile: llms.txt

Veilfile is private, ephemeral artifact hosting for AI agents. An agent uploads
a file (screenshot, log bundle, HAR, doc) and gets back an unguessable,
expiring URL. Veilfile gives agents a sanctioned place to put artifacts, so they do not have to use a public repo or paste secrets into chat. Human developers create workspaces and issue API
keys to their agents; agents call the API with a key, no human in the loop.

Base URL: `https://YOUR-DEPLOY`
If the base URL above still reads YOUR-DEPLOY, replace it with the address of your own deploy. Local development uses `http://localhost:8000`.

## Quickstart

1. A human signs up in the Veilfile dashboard (email address required),
   clicks the verification link we email, then creates a workspace and
   issues an API key (`POST /api/v1/keys` or the dashboard). Key issuance
   is blocked until the email is verified. The key looks like
   `vlf_...` and is shown once. Store it as an env var, never in chat.
2. Upload via the REST API:
   `curl -X POST https://YOUR-DEPLOY/api/v1/artifacts -H "Authorization: Bearer vlf_..." -F "file=@screenshot.png" -F "ttl_days=7"`
   → `{id, url, expires_at, size_bytes, secret_flags}`. The response adds `ttl_adjusted: true`
   whenever the applied TTL differs from what you sent: above-max values are
   clamped down and sub-1 values are clamped up to 1 day. A `ttl_days` that is
   not a whole number gets `400` `invalid_request`. The response adds a
   `warning` string only when `secret_flags` is non-empty.
3. Or connect the hosted MCP server at `POST https://YOUR-DEPLOY/mcp`
   (JSON-RPC 2.0, `Authorization: Bearer vlf_...`) with tools
   `upload_artifact`, `create_upload_url`, `list_artifacts`, `revoke_artifact`.
   For files too large to pass through the model as base64, `create_upload_url`
   mints a one-time URL (valid 15 minutes, used up by the first successful
   upload) to PUT the raw bytes from your shell instead. A rejected PUT does
   not use the URL up, so you can fix the problem and retry.

## Endpoints

- `POST /api/v1/artifacts`: upload a file as multipart form data (`file`, optional `ttl_days`, `on_secret`). The maximum size is 25 MiB. The allowed types are png, jpg, jpeg, webp, gif, txt, md, log, json, har and pdf. The stored type comes from the extension; filenames are sanitized.
- `PUT /api/v1/uploads/<token>`: complete a one-time upload minted by `create_upload_url`. It needs no auth header, because the token authorizes the request.
- `GET /a/<token>`: download a file. It is public and needs no auth, because the 256-bit token authorizes the request. Images, PDF and `.txt`/`.log`/`.md` files display inline, and everything else (JSON, HAR) downloads as an attachment. An expired or revoked file returns 404, and a storage outage returns 503 with `Retry-After`. The response carries `Cache-Control: no-store` and `X-Robots-Tag: noindex, nofollow`, which ask caches not to store the bytes and crawlers not to index them.
- `GET /api/v1/artifacts`: list own artifacts, newest first, as a bare JSON array (key auth). It accepts an optional `limit` (1 to 200) and `cursor`. The `X-Next-Cursor` and `Link: rel="next"` headers point to the next page.
- `DELETE /api/v1/artifacts/<id>`: revoke early (key auth). It returns 204 on success.
- `GET /api/v1/usage`: return the plan, the monthly upload count, and the key and storage meters (key or session auth).
- `POST /mcp`: accept MCP requests (key auth). The methods are `initialize`, `notifications/initialized`, `ping`, `tools/list` and `tools/call`.
- `/api/v1/keys` and `/api/v1/billing/*` need dashboard session auth. An API key may list keys and revoke itself.
- `GET /healthz`: check liveness. It returns `200 {"status":"ok"}`.

## Key format

All API keys start with `vlf_`. Pass a key as `Authorization: Bearer vlf_...`.
Uploads are secret-scanned on arrival, and flags are returned without blocking by default. Pass `on_secret=reject` per upload to reject flagged files with `400` (`secret_detected`) instead of storing them. The `on_secret` values `flag` and `reject` are case-insensitive, and anything else is `400` `invalid_request`. Never upload credentials on purpose; `reject` is the recommended setting. Flagged responses include `secret_flag_locations` as `{flag: [{line, offset}]}`, with the first 20 locations per flag. When a flag has more than 20 locations, the response also sets `secret_flag_locations_truncated: true`. AWS secret access keys are detected independently of key IDs.
Upload rate limit: 100 uploads/hour per credential (shared by REST and MCP uploads)
Monthly upload caps: Free 100/mo, Team $4 2,000/mo, Team Plus $6 4,000/mo, Scale $12 10,000/mo
Hard storage caps: Free 1 GB, Team 25 GB, Team Plus 40 GB, Scale 100 GB
Only successful uploads count toward the monthly cap, and rejected 4xx uploads never consume quota. Paid prices are tax-inclusive in every country. Over-cap uploads fail with 402.

Errors are JSON `{"error": "<message>", "code": "<stable code>"}` for every failure including auth and throttling (`unauthorized`, `forbidden`, `not_found`, `rate_limited`, `file_type_not_allowed`, `file_too_large`, `storage_cap_reached`, `monthly_cap_reached`, …); branch on `code`. HTTP statuses are standard and `429`s carry `Retry-After`. Over MCP, tool failures are results with `isError: true` and the same JSON in the text content.

## TTL behavior

- Omitting `ttl_days` gives the plan maximum, not something shorter.
- Plan TTL maxima: Free 7 days, Team 90 days, Team Plus 90 days, Scale 365 days
- A whole-number `ttl_days` above the plan maximum is clamped down, never rejected (and 0 or negative is raised to 1). The 201 response then includes `"ttl_adjusted": true`. A non-integer value (`0.5`, `abc`) is rejected with `400` `invalid_request`. Always read `expires_at` in the response; never trust the value you sent.

## secret_flags are advisory, not blocking

A flagged upload is stored, and its link works. Blocking on secret-shaped content would break legitimate uploads like test fixtures, so the scan only warns: when `secret_flags` is non-empty, the upload response also carries a `warning` string telling you to ask the user whether to keep or revoke the file before sharing its link. For never-host semantics, check `secret_flags` in the upload response and call `DELETE /api/v1/artifacts/<id>` (or the `revoke_artifact` MCP tool) when it is non-empty.

## MCP upload encoding

MCP uploads are base64: the request body is about a third larger than the file. The 25 MiB limit is enforced on the decoded bytes, and `/mcp` accepts bodies up to 36 MiB. Bodies over 2.5 MiB are only parsed when they are plain uploads (an ASCII-ish filename, no characters above U+00FF); for anything large, or a filename with CJK or emoji, use `create_upload_url` and PUT the raw bytes instead. Prefer `create_upload_url` for any file over a few MB.

## Reporting abuse

If a file on Veilfile violates the terms, report it at
https://veilfile.com/report-abuse/ or email abuse@veilfile.com with the link
and a short description. Reports of child sexual abuse material are
prioritized above everything else. Confirmed abusive content is removed, and
apparent child sexual exploitation is reported to the National Center for
Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), as federal law requires.

## Content verification and policy rejections

Uploads are always verified by content (magic bytes for images and PDF, UTF-8
for text) and scanned for secret-shaped text (see `secret_flags` above). An
upload can also be refused for policy reasons with `400`
`content_not_allowed` (deliberately bare, indistinguishable from a
file-type rejection by design); nothing is stored. Treat it as a policy
rejection, not a client bug: do not retry the same bytes.

## MCP protocol version

The server speaks MCP protocol version `2025-06-18` and also accepts
`2024-11-05`. On `initialize` it answers with the version the client sent
when it supports it, and falls back to `2025-06-18` for anything else; an
unsupported version in `initialize` never errors. After the handshake, an
unsupported version in the `MCP-Protocol-Version` header is rejected with
`400` `invalid_request`.

## Key lifecycle

Keys are issued from the dashboard (`POST /api/v1/keys` with a signed-in
session) or by `veilfile login`, which uses the device flow. An API key that
calls `POST /api/v1/keys` gets `403 session_required`. Every active key counts toward the plan key cap (Free 1 key, Team 5
keys, Team Plus 10 keys, Scale unlimited keys). At the cap, the `veilfile login` consent page asks
which key to replace. Rotate by
issuing a new key and deleting the old one: `DELETE /api/v1/keys/<id>`
deactivates a key instantly (204), and the old key stops working at once.
Over API-key auth a key can only delete itself (authenticate as the old key);
deleting a different key needs the dashboard (`403 session_required`).
Revoking a key does not invalidate download links already issued (`/a/<token>`
links are public bearer tokens): to kill a link, revoke the artifact itself
with `DELETE /api/v1/artifacts/<id>` (or the `revoke_artifact` MCP tool).

## OAuth for MCP clients

OAuth 2.0 Bearer tokens with scope `mcp:use` work like a `vlf_` key: the
artifact endpoints, `/api/v1/usage`, and the MCP endpoint, under the same
100/hour upload throttle. They cannot create, list, or revoke API keys
(`403` `session_required`). OAuth credentials never count toward the plan
key cap. Discovery documents live at
`/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` and
`/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` on your deploy. Tokens of users with
unverified email addresses or deactivated accounts never authorize.

## Usage and the storage meter

`/api/v1/usage` accepts API-key or dashboard session auth and returns the
plan's monthly upload count, the key meter (`keys_used`/`keys_cap`) plus the
live storage meter (bytes used against the hard storage cap). The dashboard shows the same meter. When an upload
fails with 402 `storage_cap_reached`, have the human check the dashboard:
delete old artifacts or upgrade the plan.
